stops.name: Tsingtao, Ku Hung-ming and the exiled mandarins
stops.campa: In the German colony of Tsingtao he finds the wreckage of a civilisation gathered in villas: mandarins and viceroys who fled the revolution, keeping the old rites above the new republic's reach. Among them the fiercest mind in China: Ku Hung-ming, Confucian by conviction and European by education, who defends the queue, the classics and the moral order of the ancients in flawless polemical English. Keyserling sits with the sage of Tsingtao while the old China explains itself in exile, and the diary preserves the encounter like a last audience with a dying dynasty of the spirit.

stops.name: Qufu, the grave of Confucius
stops.campa: Through Shantung he travels to Kufow, the home of Confucius, where the sage's descendants still hold their fief after seventy-five generations. In the cemetery forest of the Kung clan, under cypresses planted across two and a half millennia, he stands at the grave of the Master. No god is worshipped here; a man is remembered, and the remembering has outlasted every empire that did the forgetting. Keyserling reads the lesson of the place: a doctrine of mere decency, perfectly kept, is the most durable structure human beings have ever built.

stops.name: Peking, the Temple of Heaven
stops.campa: Peking in the first spring of the republic: the Forbidden City still houses a child emperor, abdicated but enthroned, while the vast grey city hums around the vacuum. At the Temple of Heaven Keyserling walks the empty marble circles where the Son of Heaven once answered for the harvest of the world, and grasps the enormity of what has just ended: the oldest office on earth, the priest-kingship of the cosmos, closed like a shop. The diary records Peking as grandeur in the act of becoming memory.

stops.name: Koya-san, the monastery night
stops.campa: By the Yangtse and Shanghai he crosses to Japan and climbs at once to Koya-san, the holy mountain of Shingon Buddhism. He sleeps in a monastery, wakes to sutras before dawn, and walks the Okunoin at dusk: two kilometres of tombs under giant cryptomeria, lanterns burning for the dead, at the end the hall where Kobo Daishi sits in eternal meditation, not dead, the monks say, merely absorbed. In the resin-scented dark the philosopher feels Japan's particular genius: the aesthetic and the sacred fused so perfectly that neither can be told from the other.

stops.name: Kyoto, the perfected surface
stops.campa: In Kyoto, through Nara and Ise and the temple gardens, he studies a civilisation that has made the surface profound. Fifteen stones in raked gravel; a tea bowl turned three times; the exact placement of a single iris. Japan, he writes in effect, has no metaphysics because it needs none: form itself carries the whole weight of meaning. He admires and shivers. A people this perfected in gesture, the diary notes, could pour itself into any content whatever: grace or steel. Both futures are folded in the same immaculate sleeve.

stops.name: Honolulu, the bay of Waikiki
stops.campa: Across the Pacific to Honolulu, the hinge between the hemispheres. At Waikiki he watches the surf-riders stand on the moving sea, brown bodies balancing on collapse itself, making sport of the ocean's violence, and recognises a third possibility beyond Asia's depth and Europe's will: existence as pure present-tense joy. Hawaii is the world's afternoon off. The diary relaxes here, palm-shaded, almost guilty; the philosopher permits himself paradise while the ship coals for the final continent.

stops.name: Kilauea, the fire lake
stops.campa: On Hawaii island he stands at night on the rim of Kilauea, above Halemaumau, the living lake of fire. The crust of the earth opens like a wound that glows instead of bleeding; molten rock surges, crusts, tears open again, the goddess Pele audibly breathing. For the geologist's grandson it is the primal scene itself: the third day of creation still in progress, matter not yet resigned to being mere matter. The diary records the crater as the one sermon on the journey delivered by the planet in person.

stops.name: New York, the verdict of the New World
stops.campa: Through San Francisco, the Yosemite, the Grand Canyon and Chicago he crosses America and ends at New York, where the towers stand like the will of Europe with the memory removed. He admires the energy and diagnoses the lack: a civilisation of means without inherited meaning, youth mistaking acceleration for direction. Yet the diary is not contemptuous; it is prophetic. Here, he senses, the next act of the human experiment will be staged, for better and worse. The circle is nearly closed; the Atlantic waits.

stops.name: Rayküll, the return
stops.campa: In October 1912 he walks back up the alley at Rayküll, having gone around the planet to arrive at his own door. The last chapter of the diary is written here, in the same study, by a different man: the shortest path to himself has been travelled, and its length was the equator. He settles to turn the notebooks into the book. He does not know that Europe has less than two years left, that the book will wait out a world war, and that the home he has just re-entered has already begun to vanish.

stops.name: Rayküll, the war years
stops.campa: The war seals him into his province. A Baltic German under the Russian crown, suspect to both empires, he sits at Rayküll while the fronts grind toward him, and polishes the Travel Diary that no one can print. The manor becomes an ark: inside, the manuscript of the widest journey ever taken by a German philosopher; outside, the narrowing world. Harvests fail, requisitions come, the newspapers lie in three languages. He writes on. The book about the whole earth ripens in the one place on earth he cannot leave.

stops.name: Reval (Tallinn), the leave-taking
stops.campa: Revolution takes what the war spared. Between the collapsing German occupation and the advancing Red Army, in the winter of 1918 he passes through Reval and leaves the Baltic forever. Behind him lie Könno and Rayküll, soon to be expropriated by the new Estonian republic's land reform, seven centuries of Keyserling tenure ended by statute. The aristocrat is dispossessed; and the tradition marks this as the turning, for it is precisely now, stripped of land, that he becomes wholly what he is: a man whose only estate is the spirit.

stops.name: Friedrichsruh, the Bismarck marriage
stops.campa: On 11 March 1919, in the Sachsenwald at Friedrichsruh, seat of the Iron Chancellor, the dispossessed count marries Maria Goedela Gräfin von Bismarck-Schönhausen, granddaughter of Otto von Bismarck. The tradition savours the symmetry: his grandfather Alexander was Bismarck's dearest friend at the university; two generations later the bloodlines close the circle over the wreck of both their empires. Germany is starving and in revolution; in the Bismarck house a Baltic exile weds the Chancellor's granddaughter, and a new lineage of the defeated begins.
